meta.title: Is AI ruining our skills? Early results are in and they’re not good
meta.author: jaypatelani

comments.author: inactive-user
comments.text:
I don't think it's a problem that skills can atrophy. Programmers used to be good at writing assembly on punch cards and we make do without that knowledge. But for LLMs specifically, there are three things that should give us a pause:




A lot of existing social structures are built around liability / ownership of the work product. So in some situations, you get the worst of both worlds: your ability to evaluate machine output for correctness is deteriorating the longer you use an LLM, but you still go to prison if you vibecode your taxes too much.




The skills we're talking about here are... the quintessence of the human condition? Creating art, formulating ideas, making complex decisions, expressing emotions, teaching others. So, before we reach the point where every song, painting, film, book, and blog post is coming off an LLM production line, we should try to figure out what else is there to make us proud of being humans. If the answer is "nothing", then we have some interesting choices to make.




Although AI can work as a skill multiplier, it's also a surprisingly powerful sameness multiplier: https://lcamtuf.substack.com/p/the-100000-whys-of-ai . I think it's clear that content consumers have high tolerance for sameness; AI-generated op-eds about AI now make up a significant proportion of our social feeds, and half the top-grossing films are MCU sequels, prequels, spin-offs, and remakes. But on the content production end: the tools give you an edge at the expense of stripping away all individuality. So, how do you compete in a world where your output is perfectly fungible with n billion people who can also write a prompt?



I wish we spent more time figuring this out instead of having constant "AI will cure cancer" vs "BS machines!" pie fights - which, again, are increasingly automated with LLMs.

comments.author: wrs
comments.text:
All analogies are bad, and today I’m trying this one. Bear with me, it’s a slow Sunday and the coffee hasn’t really kicked in yet.

Photography was an exciting, hyped technology. It had obvious practical benefits, but there was a strong argument that it would destroy the visual arts. Why bother spending years learning to draw and paint by hand if anybody can just point and click? And indeed, now we produce a trillion (?) photos a year, very few of which are as interesting as the average painting.

But of course the actual art wasn’t painting, it was image-making. Painting was just the last step in the process. Qualities like composition, lighting, texture, choice of subject, and — most importantly — human experience still apply to photographs. Thoughtless pointing and clicking captures an image but it doesn’t make art.

“Artless” photos aren’t useless; they’re great for documenting parties, remembering that you once saw the Golden Gate Bridge, and millions of other things you would never have commissioned a painting of. But we all see that those are in a different category.

Artistic and practical images used to be done by the same highly educated people using the same techniques, and both used to be expensive and rare. Photography democratized the technique and made practical images essentially free to create, but the fundamental skills required to make an artistic image are pretty much the same as ever. And I’d guess the auction value of a good original artwork remains higher than a good photograph.

comments.author: emk
comments.text:
Some of the underlying anxiety here is that these models are barely 4 years old, and we've gone from "can sort of write a factorial function" to "can one-shot a 3D adventure game demo, complete with quest-givers." Or "Can one shot a custom (toy) programming language."

And I remember what I read about horses. The first steam engines were wildly impractical, and they were basically only used in coal mines because coal is nearly free in a mine. Obviously, they weren't going to replace horses.

And in fact, the horse population went up for decades after the introduction of the steam engine. But eventually, various sorts of internal combustion engines became an almost fully general replacement for horses. And the horse population dropped.

So now I wonder, how many more years will it be before we build a fully-general replacement for the human mind? And what would happen then?

I may complain about the quality of Fable's code. But it can complete medium-sized projects end-to-end in a couple of hours for a few hundred dollars. And no, it isn't quite yet a fully general replacement for the human mind. But it's another big step closer.

Replacing your paintbrush with a camera isn't quite the same thing as replacing your own mind with something that thinks for you. That's a step where I fear analogies will begin to fail.

comments.author: wrs
comments.text: So far, as someone who uses LLMs extensively, they are nowhere near thinking for me. They have no idea what to do until I prompt them, and no way to judge the result unless I tell them how. Much like my camera.

comments.author: esak
comments.text: The consensus (outside of disconnected management, ai-pilled true-believers, and marketing-savvy CEOs) seems to be that LLMs aren’t, currently, and likely won’t be, capable as “a fully general replacement for the human mind”. Whether or not “fully general” is possible remains debatable (e.g., substrate independent consciousness is still squarely the stuff of sci-fi). However, LLMs and agent-based workflows are clearly a step in the direction of wholesale automated cognition - a point that the TFA makes and that the parent touches on. The more you leverage them to solve your problems in some domain, the more your own problem-solving skills to atrophy in that domain. As that domain specificity gives way, so too will your problem solving skills more broadly. It takes something a lot less than “a fully general replacement of the human mind” to become a crutch that wrecks your ability to solve hard problems on your own. You can use a calculator, horseless carriage, or camera analogy, but the idea of “intelligence on tap” strikes me as a net loss in some sense.

comments.author: emk
comments.text:
The Culture sounds nice when we're talking loosely about something we don't really believe will happen within our lifetimes (or our children's).

But once I started to consider the possibility that we might be doing this, for real, then it got a lot more complicated. I can see two basic scenarios if AI advances that far:


Someone builds a Culture Mind that obeys humans. But then the natural question arises: Which humans? Not us, obviously. Probably some politician or CEO. Who would have the kind of power associated with, well, Culture Minds. Which are the next best thing to gods, when you get right down to it. I'm pretty sure that any future where a politician or lab CEO has a pet Culture Mind is going to be a nightmare dystopia. And indeed, we're already seeing the first models restricted to government-approved users only.

Or maybe someone builds a Culture Mind that doesn't particularly listen to humans. At this point, you have a high risk of, well, SkyNet. Or if you're really unlucky (and if remember your old science fiction), the Blight.


The idea that some assholes in Silicon Valley actually wish, for real, to gamble my children's future on trying to build a damn "machine god" fills me with rage. It stops being fun the moment I realize the lab CEOs mean the stuff they say. At least if you think there's even a slight chance of it actually happening.

Happily (for now) there are at least a few things they haven't figured out yet. Not that they won't spend trillions of dollars trying.

comments.author: emk
comments.text:
Yeah, personally I only take "The State of the Art" as semi-canonical. I believe it was the first written and the continuity feels slightly off in places, if I remember correctly.

And when I say "human" in the context of the Culture, feel free to substitute "approximately 6 major natural species, plus later additions, plus massive genetic overhauls by the Minds, plus the human-equivalent sentient drones." The drone Churt Lyne, for all intents and purposes, can be lumped with the Culture "humans", rather than the Minds. Churt Lyne is an approximately human-level AGI, a normal participant in society, and a moral patient.

If our society's plans for AI were limited to entities like Churt Lyne or Data—non-massively-replicated, physically embodied minds of roughly human capabilities—I would have far fewer worries. Such entities could potentially participate in society without breaking it beyond repair.

My concern with people hoping to build Culture-like Minds is that it would represent power that would be nearly impossible for baseline human beings to hold to account. Whether the machine obeys some random trillionaire or only itself, it would still be an unaccountable power. And maybe history and/or recent decades have made me cynical, but I don't trust humans with that kind of power.

comments.author: inactive-user
comments.text:
Correct me if I misunderstood what you're saying, but I think you might be making two arguments in defense of the tech, right? The first one is that AI is just another tool for creative expression - just how photography supplanted paintings, but didn't kill visual arts. The second argument may be that not all uses of technology need to serve an artistic purpose, just how a photo can be useful even if it's not good.

If I'm reading this right, I think it's somewhat tangential to what I'm trying to say: I'm not rejecting AI, I'm just saying that it is different in ways that should probably give us a pause.

But to address your points, I don't disagree with #2. LLMs have plenty of beneficial uses; my subjective POV as an old-fashioned internet user is that I encounter negative externalities more often than I benefit from the tech, but I accept that it's different for other folks. For #1, I get it in theory, but I'm not seeing it in practice, probably because the creation of wholesale AI art doesn't leave a whole lot of room for individualistic perspective or learned skill. You're just writing a short prompt; further, prompt generation can be automated with an LLM too. Do human prompts have a "spark" that a machine could never approximate? I don't know... maybe for now?

comments.author: ewintr
comments.text:
For #1, I get it in theory, but I'm not seeing it in practice, probably because the creation of wholesale AI art doesn't leave a whole lot of room for individualistic perspective or learned skill. You're just writing a short prompt;


The point of art is not (only) to make a picture or text of a certain quality, it is also a means of expression or communication. You cannot put any meaningful amount of expression in a short prompt. Or rather you can, similar to a short story, but then the prompt itself already would qualify as art and it would have taken skill and effort to write.

In my work as a developer, I am a big user of AI, to the point that the lines of code I've written by hand last year could fit on a few sheets of paper. When writing short stories however, I have found LLMs completely useless. Apart from the fact that they cannot write interesting stories, only cliches, they simply cannot write my stories, because those have to come from within me.

Writing is the process of unearthing what lives inside my mind. I could do the same unearthing to provide prompt material, but what would be the point? It is more work and the result would be worse. One day there will be a young artist who uses LLMs as a tool to create art, I am sure of it, but it will definitely be more involved than 'just a short prompt.'

On #1, the analogy is that the result from a short prompt is like a point and shoot picture. You didn’t put any effort into it, you just wanted to get a quick result. And we all know it when we see the picture. That can be useful, but it’s not art.

My real-life pursuits are software, music, and a little bit of photography, and in all three areas I currently seem to have no trouble distinguishing between the result of a one-shot brief AI prompt and a lengthy session of a human using AI assistance.

Assertions that humans are replaceable at a high level just seem unfounded to me. That’s not to say we won’t see a lot more artless machine-generated artifacts, just like we see a lot of artless photos.

(Edit for clarity: I’m not “defending the tech”, and in no way trivializing or dismissing the vast uncertainties and concern here — just trying to relate it to a process that’s been going on long enough to characterize with some perspective.)

comments.text:
The details depend on the medium of course, but (assuming the problem is deep enough to be worth talking about in the first place) you can look at the output and usually see whether it's a shallow solution made with a bunch of arbitrary choices, or something with thought behind it. Basically, if I ask a lot of questions about the solution, will they have reasonable answers in terms of professional practice? Does the thing fit well into the existing context, or does it look like something that just arrived from somewhere else and got pasted on?

As a random example, look at the current panoply of identical-looking dark-mode home pages filled with emojis and feature bullets. It doesn't take a huge amount of discernment to know that these folks did not sit down and think "what is the most effective design for my website?". They didn't even sit down with Claude and say "let's discuss the most effective design for my website". They just said "hey Claude, build me a website".

comments.author: rjzak
comments.text:
Maybe to restate:


If you're not a programmer, AI is great because you can make a great app, a great game without having the background in computer science to be able to make it without AI. A friend of mine recently showed me his iOS app he made but he's not a iOS/Mac developer. AI allowed him to do something that would have taken him months to learn, but he did it in a few days. This is democratizing software development, allowing a non-programmer to make a program they're proud of.

If you're a programmer and you start offloading more and more thinking and software development to the AI, the skills atrophy, and maybe you get lazy and don't review the quality or ensure that the tests are meaningful (or are even there). It's human nature to get lazy when that's an option. This is bad, loss of skill and quality, perhaps in a corporate setting. Then the quality declines and perhaps customers are lost.

comments.author: wrs
comments.text:
One of the important aspects of the analogy is the question: Is that really a "great game"?

If the person is a great game designer, but just doesn't know the iOS SDK, then it might be. Just as if someone was a great graphic designer, but didn't know how to use Illustrator, they could team up with someone else to make a great digital design.

But if the person isn't a great game designer, that's probably not a great game. The new ability to easily make an app doesn't make you a game designer. Making the app used to be hard, but that wasn't the "essential hardness" of the problem. Not having to grind your own pigment probably unblocked a few new great visual artists, but not many.

comments.author: rjzak
comments.text: Sure, there is still the issue of creativity, inspiration, and work ethic. Someone could make that great game by first making bad games, then mediocre versions, then great. But it's also subjective, great to one person isn't going to be great to another.

comments.author: wrs
comments.text:
This is getting into "The Quality Without a Name" territory, but sure, there is a big subjective component. It is a good additional point though: Someone gains the ability to make better games by making a lot of worse games first. And reducing the effort involved in making those games may well accelerate their progress toward greatness, not render them unable to become great.

I think part of what we're wrestling with here (and have done for thousands of years) is whether removing some of the effort required makes it "too easy" for people to get good at the thing. If you don't have to "pay your dues" first then do you "deserve" to be great? But that's oversimplified — part of what you're doing when you "pay your dues" is gaining experience with the medium and building intuition and tacit knowledge about how it works. You have to gain that knowledge somehow; you can't just skip over it. If you do, you aren't going to actually be good at the thing.

In photography, one is forced to learn a lot about values and dynamic range while setting a manual camera, then developing the film, then making prints. With digital, one still has to learn about values and dynamic range, though it's done very differently. You don't get to skip it just because the camera and software are removing some of the mechanical steps.

(edited slightly for clarity)

comments.author: bsder
comments.text:
Although AI can work as a skill multiplier, it's also a surprisingly powerful sameness multiplier


AI always pulls to the median. Always.

I have had several projects where I'm configuring: "These are unusual engineering decisions but they are correct and immutable: A, B, C.  Do not violate them.*

ALL of the AIs systems will try to rewrite the code with the "median" solution.  All of them will sooner or later try to rip out those engineering decisions and replace them with the median solution--even when the median solution is wrong.

And this is responsible for most of the "genuine" AI disconnect, I think.  If "median" code is fine, then AI is probably at least okay.  Anyone below the median thinks AIs are universally useful.  Those of us above the median in some area see just how garbagey AI is in that area.  Combine that with a dose of Gell-Mann Amnesia Effect and you can see where this is going.

And that's if I just completely ignore all the AI-hypesters and con-artists trying to make a quick buck.

comments.author: scraps
comments.text:
I think it's clear that content consumers have high tolerance for sameness; AI-generated op-eds about AI now make up a significant proportion of our social feeds


The latter isn't really evidence of the former; the fact that something is in your feed isn't necessarily a sign of success. I'm under the impression engagement numbers on social media are down, not up, and that the preponderance of AI content is making people pull back from social media. Social media seems to be losing cultural relevance, not gaining.

Using the volume of content as evidence is a confusion of cause and effect. The content in a user's feed is the cause. The desired effect is the user's behavior from consuming the feed. Let's say the content is short videos of people telling jokes in front of brick walls at comedy clubs. The thing to measure isn't the number of clips: it's the number of laughs.

In your blog post you use number of books on Amazon as an example. In that scenario, the number of books is actually the input, not the output: the output is purchases, not books. Gary Marcus wrote about this exact example recently: the number of books on Amazon has gone up, but the number of book sales has gone down over the same period.  https://garymarcus.substack.com/p/slop-productivity-and-why-the-ai

comments.author: k749gtnc9l3w
comments.text:
So, before we reach the point where every song, painting, film, book, and blog post is coming off an LLM production line, we should try to figure out what else is there to make us proud of being humans.


Careful with that question. Even without asking about LLMs, what is there now to make us proud of being humans, full stop, no in-group restriction? How many people would already answer «nothing»?

As a decades-old observation goes, intelligence needed to bring down the civilisation goes down, and the intelligence needed to see a reason «why not» goes up. LLMs might have accelerated one or both of the trends, but surely haven't started either. Although, there is a risk of moving the crossover point quite a bit closer.


tools give you an edge at the expense of stripping away all individuality


There are many dimensions, and one chooses which to give up.


perfectly fungible with n billion people who can also write a prompt


On the one hand there are people who would meaningfully compete on prompt.

On the flip side it is a bit of Hollywood problem, at least in English, given that AO3 and Jamendo and… DeviantArt, I guess? seem to provide practically unbounded amount of no-charge-for-personal-enjoyment art, with best examples very well done and probably with wider range of originality than commercial offerings.

I still regret the loss of «sort by popularity, skip to the last page» on Jamendo, fallen at the hand of infiniscroll. Being good at being popular comes at a price, sequel-itis just put it under a sharper light, and artificial-neural-net models might simply increase the contrast yet a bit more. But for the consumption types where current popularity-optimised stuff is suitable, maybe a flow will be found where people won't mind anyway?

comments.author: k749gtnc9l3w

Training formally is not the question, there are manuals and all, more like mentor along the way.

At 6 months maybe, in six months spent learning and practicing a single topic one can learn a lot. 6 person-months full-time might be competitive with what some places spent on starting to use those machines on the base of general competence in mathematics and engineering, not sure!

I wouldn't overestimate transferability of everything: a lot of good uses of those machines is in numerical approximations (not everyone's specialisation nowadays…), and a lot of modern optimisation techniques are not needed on a more sequential setup (and compute/throughput balance has changed even its shape so many times by now!) One of them was substring search, which I obviously implemented naively. comments.author: emk
comments.text:
I discussed a related issue in my weekend update here on Lobsters. Basically, I just refuse to do blind vibecoding for anything beyond throwaway experiments. If I commit something, I want to understand it, and to be happy with the quality. And during the few days I used Fable, I wasn't happy with the quality of the code it wrote: There were lots of subtly-cut corners, tons of code to silently recover from things that should have been treated as invariant violations, and a tendency to throw another thousand lines of code at the wall instead of teasing out an actual architecture. For some kinds of software, sure, you can get away with this. But for the core infrastructure that does the heavy lifting, I don't think it's wise.

But there are some serious problems with relying too heavily on the models:


Reading code will never produce the same depth of insight that writing it does.

A series of individually plausible-looking PRs can add up to a real hairball of code.

Popular wisdom says that reading code is harder than writing it.


And so I'm realizing that while I'm OK with some AI, I really want to spend a lot more time with my hands on the keyboard, and with my understanding fully engaged. As I noted in my earlier post, my personal sweet spot is somewhere between Qwen3.6 27B and DeepSeek V4 Flash. Which is, coincidentally, about the size range of models that a programmer could run locally if fast RAM were cheaper.

Fable, well, I'm really concerned. It does far more "mostly OKish" work than any human could ever hope to understand or review. Not sure where this will end up.

comments.author: deemas
comments.text:
Computer technology throughout its short history has been a great accelerator.

Engelbart, of "The Mother of All Demos" fame predicted that measures of computer assisted human performance would increase exponentially as we used computers to create tools to make computers better. He was right and I think we have entered this sort of 'singularity like' period where in a few decades humans have progressed technically and economically farther than all previous progress recorded in 6 thousand years of written history.

It's not a true singularity Kurzweil style because because that is just bookselling marketing. But it has been a real, historical change in civilization. And for the past few decades, all this power has been giving some people and organizations amounts of resource that enabled them to basically do anything they wanted. Most, if not all, chose to enrich themselves. We now have a trillionaire, someone who owns basically ~5% of the US monetary supply.

This level of growth and resource availability reveals what sort of person those with access to these levers really are. I won't pass judgement, but I think it is a naked reality for all to see what the people who have for the past few decades who received these opportunities have chosen to do.

Computers accelerate humans, they compress time. It is still our choice what to do with it. It is a bit saddening that so many have chosen basic garden variety greed, just to orders of magnitude previously undreamed of.

We all can chose what to do with these levers. Do you want to exert yourself less, to get more money, a bigger house? Do you want to build something? What do you want to do?

At this junction in time, an epochal change is taking place. Our choices reveal our nature, our desires bound us and at the same time our choices can liberate us. But don't think this is some new thing, or some unknown future awaits us. This is the same fork on the road we keep coming back to, we always have and always will. This is what consciousness: a journey which constitutes of learning and choosing what to do with what we learn, and reaping the consequences, rinse repeat.

Chose well.
